item.title: What questions and debates in Parliament say about India’s climate change priorities
item.description: There was a focus on energy and forests but financial and institutional dimensions of climate action were less examined.
item.content:encoded:
India, like other countries, is grappling with the effects of El Niño, which has exacerbated global warming, causing a major rainfall deficit in the country this year. Over the past decade, India has seen climate change take a deadly toll in the form of extreme weather and disasters such as landslides and glacial collapse.

How did these concerns resonate in the Indian Parliament?

In the last 10 years, Parliament maintained a steady focus on climate change, but its attention has centered largely on setting ambitious goals and announcing national targets.

My analysis of the environmental-related questions discussed in Parliament over the last 10 years found that the focus was on sectors such as energy and forests. The financial and institutional dimensions of climate action received considerably less attention.

The report titled “Climate on the Floor: India’s Parliamentary Discourse on Environment since the Paris Agreement” was released by the Centre for Financial Accountability on October 2. It analysed the questions raised in Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha between December 2015 and December 2025, along with parliamentary debates. India was among the 200 countries that adopted the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement on reducing carbon emissions.

item.title: Three years since October 7, Gaza has faded from headlines. All eyes are now on Israel’s elections
item.description: If a less extreme government takes office after the polls on October 27, will the world’s attention to Gaza and the West Bank hold?
item.content:encoded:
This week marks three years since Hamas’ massacre of October 7, 2023, in which some 1,200 people, most of them Israeli civilians, were killed and 251 taken hostage.

What followed were two years of devastating war waged by the Israel Defense Forces in Gaza, which a United Nations commission of inquiry, leading genocide scholars and major human rights organisations have concluded amounted to genocide. Much of the strip lies in ruins and more than 74,000 Palestinians are dead, with thousands more believed to remain buried under the rubble.

A year ago this week, a US-imposed ceasefire was finally forced on both sides – though mainly on paper. While major IDF assaults have ceased, Israeli attacks in Gaza have continued, in addition to unbridled Jewish settler violence in the West Bank.

Despite this, global attention on Gaza has waned. As the US-Israeli war with Iran began dominating the headlines, earlier pledges by many states to help drive the peace process forward have proved once again wanting, even hollow.

Now, Israel is preparing for a highly polarised parliamentary election on October 27, which could be consequential for the entire region. If a less extreme government takes office, will the world’s attention to Gaza and the West Bank – and the pressure it has generated – hold?

item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Red Wind Howls’, by Tsering Döndrup, translated by Christopher Peacock.

Alak Drong, the lama whose honorific prefix was paired with the rather unusual name “Drong” – Wild Yak – was sporting a pair of black crystal sunglasses on the bridge of his nose and a gold ring inlaid with an agate stone on his left ring finger. As usual, he was wearing a brown Chinese suit, which, in cold weather, was always complemented by a dark red fur coat with a lynx collar. At first glance, you might think he was a rich, uncouth businessman. But on closer inspection, the shortcropped hair, the collar of a yellow cotton undershirt poking out from his suit, and the simple rosary wrapped around his left wrist made clear to anyone with even a passing familiarity with Tibet that he belonged to the ranks of lamas and reincarnations who, in those years, so terrifying when we look back on them, had come unstuck from their sacred vows like a snake unwinding its coils or a cap popping off a beer bottle.

item.title: Henri Kagan, Kenso Soai win chemistry Nobel for research into mirror-image molecules
item.description: Discoveries by them have been ‘decisive’ for developing pharmaceuticals, said the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded on Wednesday to two chemists for their research into the mirror images of molecules, which is decisive for the development of pharmaceuticals.

Henri Kagan, 95, is a professor at the Université Paris-Sud in France. He is a French citizen. Kenso Soai, a 76-year-old Japanese citizen, is a professor at the Tokyo University of Science.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said that they were being honoured for the discovery of “non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.

Some molecules, such as amino acids, exist as two variants that are each other’s mirror image. However, living organisms only contain one of these mirror images.

“How chemical asymmetry such as this could have emerged was long a mystery to chemists,” the academy said, adding that Kagan and Soai discovered “a solution to this puzzle”.

Their discoveries have been “decisive for chemists who design reactions” for manufacturing pharmaceuticals, it added.

The two chemists will equally share the prize amount of 12 million Swedish kronor, or Rs 11.5 crore.

The Nobel Prize in literature will be announced on Thursday and for peace on Friday. The prize in economics will be announced on October 12.

The Constitutional Conduct Group said it felt compelled to write the open letter “at a juncture in our country’s history when constitutional values are being openly breached, and when democratic dialogue and discussion are virtually absent, with any expression of dissent or difference of opinion being termed ‘anti-national’”.

The group urged serving bureaucrats to uphold their “primary allegiance” to the Constitution and follow the law even when doing so causes “personal inconvenience”.

They described the Election Commission’s handling of the special intensive revision of voter rolls as the “most glaring example of wilful disregard of constitutional ethics”.

item.title: Semiconductors are driving the global economy. A new book looks at its human and environmental costs
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Chip Age: How Semiconductors Became the World’s Most Powerful Resource’, by Rakesh Kumar.
item.content:encoded:
Accidents aren’t the only thing that can cause the release of chipmaking toxins into the environment. Routine handling of chemicals during chipmaking can also lead to exposure, with serious health consequences. Perhaps the most famous case was the discovery of the significant impact of photoresists – a type of chemical critical to chip manufacturing – on the reproductive health of female chip factory workers – a discovery that started when an observant graduate student was looking for a thesis adviser.

In 1984, when Harris Pastides was an associate professor of epidemiology at the University of Massachusetts in Amherst, he was contacted by James Stewart, a graduate student who was looking for both a graduate adviser and a thesis topic. Stewart was also a health and safety officer at the Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC), a chip company that sold microprocessors.

He had noticed that several pregnant employees at the company’s Hudson plant – where many women worked in chip production and were thus routinely exposed to various chemicals used in the chip production process – had experienced miscarriages. item.title: RBI raises repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% amid rising inflation
item.description: This was the first hike in the lending rate in four years.
item.content:encoded:
The Reserve Bank of India on Wednesday increased the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5%.

The repo rate is the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks. The Monetary Policy Committee reviews the rate every two months.

This was the first hike in the lending rate in nearly four years. The last hike was in February 2023, when the Reserve Bank of India raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 6.5%.

Central banks usually increase key lending rates to control inflation. Higher key lending rates translate to higher interest on loans disbursed by commercial banks. This, in turn, keeps a check on discretionary spending by consumers which is expected to help curb price rise due to high inflation.

The committee had cut the repo rate by 25 basis points from 5.5% to 5.25% in December and kept it unchanged in February, April, June and August.

A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Basis points are used to describe changes in interest rates and other financial instruments.

The committee also changed its monetary policy stance to “calibrated tightening” from “neutral”. The shift signals that the central bank is now more focused on containing inflation.

item.title: How Netanyahu and Modi turn security failures into political weapons
item.description: Their strategy is to make citizens more afraid of the enemy than angry with the government that failed them.
item.content:encoded:
The passengers aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv survived because a wounded captain, some passengers and reserve pilots prevented a disaster.

When they returned to Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was there to welcome them. It was a perfect opportunity for photographs: Netanyahu standing beside passengers of a plane who had escaped death. Missing from the public discussion was the question his government needed to answer. Why had their survival depended on a heavily injured pilot doing what a robust security system should have made unnecessary?

The September 30 flight had come close to disaster when its Omani copilot, Hamam al-Hammami, allegedly attacked the Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, with a crash axe. Despite his injuries, Machchhar opened the cockpit door, reportedly allowing passengers to overpower the attacker. The aircraft eventually safely landed in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

item.title: Saeed Naqvi on being the first journalist to interview Nelson Mandela after his release from jail
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The World Was Not Their Story: An Odyssey of an Indian Reporter’.

The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 signalled the end of the Soviet Union. This, in its wake, unfroze conflicts across the globe that were sustained by the West in the Cold War. I remember how Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and other Commonwealth leaders failed to persuade Britain’s Margaret Thatcher at a 1986 summit in London to stiffen sanctions against apartheid. Thatcher’s reaction was rigid because the Soviet paranoia still plagued the West. That is why she advanced a lame excuse for not weakening the White apartheid regime.

“More sanctions would hurt Black workers,” she argued.

Likewise, Italy’s Christian Democrats were kept in power despite unspeakable corruption, much of which came to light only after the Soviet threat had ended in 1991. Under one of its most popular leaders, Enrico Berlinguer, the Italian Communist Party had distanced itself from Moscow and adopted a more moderate line, but remained a formidable electoral threat to the Christian Democrats. In the years that followed, Yugoslavia would break apart and the five Central Asian republics of the Soviet Union would emerge as independent states. item.title: Ethiopia is slipping into a war again that could expand to more countries
item.description: The conflicts will intersect with the civil war in neighboring Sudan, causing a complicated, regionwide conflagration.
item.content:encoded:
Four years after a fragile ceasefire ended widespread conflict in Ethiopia, the region is again slipping back into full-out war.

On September 23, 2026, advancing soldiers of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front seized government positions in northern Ethiopia.

It followed the announcement of a new alliance of seven armed movements in opposition to the Ethiopian government and deteriorating relations between the country and neighboring Eritrea, which it accuses of supporting the new alliance.

As an expert on conflict in the Horn of Africa and Ethiopian national security, I know the spiraling conditions now have been long in the making.

The November 2022 Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement ended immediate fighting between Ethiopia and Tigrayan rebels, but it did not constitute a comprehensive peace settlement. Crucially, it was never followed by wider political negotiations to address the root causes of the war. The concern now is that the conflicts will intersect with the civil war in neighboring Sudan, causing a complicated, regionwide conflagration.

How has the conflict escalated?

item.title: Bangladesh measles outbreak claims 900 lives – and serves as warning for why vaccination matters
item.description: Even a small dip in vaccination rates can leave pockets of unprotected children.
item.content:encoded:
Almost 900 people in Bangladesh are suspected to have died in a measles outbreak that began in March. Most of those affected are children.

Measles is one of the most infectious diseases known. It can spread rapidly when vaccination rates fall, and the Bangladesh outbreak shows how quickly years of gaps in protection can turn into a serious public health crisis.

The country had hoped to eliminate measles and rubella by 2020. Instead, the pandemic disrupted routine childhood vaccinations, leaving pockets of children vulnerable to the virus. Now other countries where vaccination rates have fallen face a similar risk.

Vaccine hesitancy is probably part of the story here too. During the Covid pandemic, almost half of Bangladesh’s population were wary of getting vaccinated. That same wariness may well have carried over to the measles-rubella jab, with many parents simply refusing to let their children be vaccinated.

Measles has its own set of drivers, too. Poverty, education levels, and how often mothers attend antenatal check-ups all shape whether children in a community end up vaccinated. Add it all up, and childhood vaccination coverage has been sliding for years – down to just 87%.

item.title: Francis Halzen awarded physics Nobel for discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin
item.description: His ‘vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental’ for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, said the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Prize in Physics was on Tuesday awarded to Belgian physicist Francis Halzen for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin and his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.

Halzen, 82, is a professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in the United States.

“His vision and scientific leadership have been fundamental for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors,” the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.

The observatory is near the South Pole in Antarctica. Using the observatory, researchers “can capture neutrinos from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe”, the academy added.

Halzen first presented his vision for capturing neutrinos at the South Pole in 1988. When a neutrino collides with an atomic nucleus, it produces a flash of light that can be tracked by sensors in the glacial ice.

He will receive a prize amount of 12 million Swedish krona, or Rs 11.5 crore.

On Monday, the Nobel Prize in medicine was jointly awarded to three scientists – Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth – for their research on brain activity.

The Nobel Prize in chemistry will be announced on Wednesday, literature on Thursday and for peace on Friday. The prize in economics will be announced on October 12.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s much-discussed special address at Davos in January called for a world of “values-based realism.” First proposed by Finland’s President, Alexander Stubb, values-based realism describes not a strategy, but an “instrument – temporary, adaptive, and situational…that espouses values while engaging respectfully with those who do not share them.”

Put more colloquially, this macro-geopolitical landscape operates exactly like a Gen Z “situationship” – relationships that are not beholden to labels, exclusivity, and can be non-committal.

While wider biomedical discourses focus on the laparoscope’s convenience, rural women often resist this simplistic understanding and draw on their everyday lives to develop an understanding of how this technology works. The way that the laparoscope enters everyday conversations of rural Rajasthani women – what it is, how it works and whether it is better than open surgery – uncovers women’s relationships with population control efforts, the fascination with technology, and power exercised by the state and biomedical institutions. item.title: How El Niño is causing droughts in parts of the world and floods elsewhere
item.description: It is a result of climactic conditions being shaped by the warming Pacific Ocean and the air above it.
item.content:encoded:
The Pacific Ocean is warming unusually quickly, and this year’s El Niño has already surpassed previous records. Forecasters expect it to strengthen even further before approaching its usual peak around December.

El Niño, the warm phase of a natural fluctuation in the Earth’s climate system, can reshape weather thousands of miles away, bringing drought to some regions while increasing the risk of heavy rain and flooding in others. To understand why, you need to follow what happens to the Pacific’s warm water – and the air above it.

Usually, winds over the tropical Pacific blow from east to west, pushing warm surface water towards the western Pacific, where it piles up around Indonesia and nearby regions. These are the trade winds. As warm water moves westward, colder water from deeper in the ocean rises to replace it in the east – a process called upwelling. This is why the western Pacific is usually much warmer than the eastern Pacific.

item.title: Nobel Prize in Medicine awarded to three scientists for brain research

The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was on Monday jointly awarded to three scientists for their work on light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.

Peter Hegemann from Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel from the University of Würzburg in Germany discovered a protein, named channelrhodopsin, in a single-celled alga.

Karl Deisseroth from The Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University in the United States developed a way to turn the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells.

Their research has fundamentally changed the way science understands the human brain, the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet said in a statement. The three scientists have “laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience”, it added.

Their research has led to the discovery of a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviours in the brain, the Nobel Assembly said.

Researchers are using the method to try and restore eyesight in people.

“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, the chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine.

The three scientists will equally share the prize amount of 12 million Swedish krona, or Rs 11.5 crore.

The mob also scuffled with the police while trying to enter the campus, reported The Indian Express.

Rohit Shaw, a spokesperson for the Hindutva group, was quoted as saying by The Telegraph that the Bangiyo Hindu Jagaran Manch carried out the march because students of the institute had “disrespected the image of Swami Vivekananda and Bharat Mata” on September 27.

On that day, at least six students were injured after being attacked for objecting to an event organised by members of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh-affiliated consumer group Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat.

At least one of those injured was hit on the head and another was allegedly attacked with a knife, a student told Scroll.

The RSS, a Hindutva organisation, is the ideological parent of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

Poorvi Bondre, a member of the union, had told Deutsche Welle that students confronted participants of the event after learning that the organisers were affiliated with the RSS and using the event to “promote its agenda” on campus.

item.title: Why an anonymous X post about anti-caste readings got the PMO’s attention
item.description: Most of the works cited in the X post contain arguments critical of the caste system and, in some instances, Hindutva.

Periyar EV Ramasamy, one of the leading figures of the Dravidian movement, argued that “To insist that chastity is only for women and should not be insisted upon for men, is a philosophy based on biased individual ownership.” As part of the argument, published in his Collected Works, he noted further that “If our literatures have all been written for the sake of justice and disciplined conduct, then, should not all the conditions imposed on women be applied to men too.”

To many academics, these arguments remain relevant and vital even today, and students stand to gain significantly from reading and engaging with them. To their shock, however, the book was among the publications that the Prime Minister’s Office took note of after an anonymous X user included it in a list of material that the user termed “poison”.

item.title: Can a messy person change or are some people just naturally tidier?
item.description: Personality isn’t destiny and changing patterns may eventually change something about the kind of person we are.
item.content:encoded:
Some people seem naturally tidy. Their keys are always in the same place, clothes make it into the wardrobe, and their kitchen bench remains mysteriously visible.

Others can clean the house on Sunday and wonder by Wednesday how everything became messy again.

It’s tempting to explain this as personality: “I’m just a messy person.” And there is some truth to that. But personality isn’t destiny. Our surroundings and the small things we repeatedly do within them matter too.

In fact, changing those patterns may eventually change something about the kind of person we are.

Are some people just naturally tidier?

Psychologists describe personality in terms of relatively enduring patterns in how people tend to think, feel and behave.

One of the “Big Five” personality traits is conscientiousness. It includes tendencies towards being industrious, self-controlled and orderly. So, someone higher in conscientiousness – particularly its orderliness aspects – may find keeping things organised easier.

But “relatively enduring” doesn’t mean personality is fixed.

Large studies following people over time show personality is both stable and changeable. For example, people tend to become more conscientious during different stages of adulthood, such as when they have children or new responsibilities.

So, saying “I’m a messy person” may describe a tendency. It doesn’t condemn you to a lifetime of losing your keys.

item.title: How a love of gossip could make you a better reader
item.description: The intimacies and power dynamics navigated through a novel can be decoded by using the same skills we exercise when we gossip.
item.content:encoded:
In case you missed it, Rachel Cusk’s new novel Life of M has been the centre of heated online debate. Dubbed a “biogossip” (biography based on gossip) allegedly inspired by the actress Natalie Portman, the novel investigates fame, power and truth with a particular emphasis on storytelling.

Much of the discussion of the book revolves around the similarities between Portman’s real life rather than how Cusk explores her chosen themes. In a recent article for The Guardian, journalist Elle Hunt provides a handy list of must-know information for those wishing to read the novel but may be unsure of all the details. The biogossip argument is certainly plausible. For instance, references to Léon: The Professional (1994) and Black Swan (2010) are easy enough to pick up if you are aware of Portman’s filmography. At the conclusion, Hunt asks whether more gossip in literature could solve the crisis of people reading less than ever.

Sharing insider knowledge

It is interesting to consider whether easy-to-spot references to public figures are the key to drawing new readers in. However, asking for more gossip may be addressing the symptoms rather than the cause and ignores the fact that gossip has always existed in literature, and to a far greater extent than you might think.

item.title: These websites give you the thrill of online shopping without buying anything
item.description: A new trend emerging in South Korea allows users to browse products, place and order and even track its ‘delivery’.
item.content:encoded:
This article was originally published in Rest of World, which covers technology’s impact outside the West.

This week, I placed orders for a $44,860 Patek Philippe hand-engraved watch, a $12,500 Hermès handbag, a $9,800 Tiffany diamond ring, and a $7,350 Cartier Love bracelet in yellow gold.

I don’t need any of them. I certainly can’t afford them. Thankfully, they’ll never arrive.

Instead of Amazon, I spent the past week browsing a new breed of websites known as “dopamine sites,” a trend that emerged in South Korea. These websites – like Dopamine Shop and FoodNeverComes – recreate the entire ritual of online shopping: You search for products, compare reviews, add items to your cart, enter a shipping address, place an order, and even track your delivery.

Then … nothing happens. No money changes hands. No package arrives.

It’s tempting to dismiss them as another quirky internet trend. But after spending a week placing imaginary orders, I found myself wondering if online shopping has stopped being solely about buying things.

item.title: Sunday book pick: Simone de Beauvoir’s ‘A Very Easy Death’ is a moving memoir about her dying mother
item.description: The memoir was originally published in French in 1964 as ‘Une Morte Très Douce.’ It was translated by Patrick O’Brian in 1965.
item.content:encoded:
“Her heart was in excellent condition and her blood pressure was that of a young woman: I had never been afraid of a sudden mishap for her.”

Simone de Beauvoir’s A Very Easy Death, a memoir about her dying mother, is the perfect read if you’re looking to fill a Mother Mary Comes to Me-sized hole in your heart.

An age to die

Beauvoir begins the story of her mother Françoise’s death with the news of her breaking the neck of her femur after a fall in the bathroom. Her neighbours call her daughters, Simone and Poupette, who immediately rush to the scene. Françoise is addressed as maman by her daughters and at 77, Beauvoir reasons that she is of an “age to die.” The hospital stay is longer than they expected, and the nurses help maman to eat, wash, and go to the bathroom. Beauvoir watches a swarm of people attending to her mother. Maman, who used to dress with consciousness, is made to wear nighties and is undressed several times a day as every nurse goes about her duty. Beauvoir is “jarred” by her mother’s nakedness, by how small and vulnerable she is.

item.title: ‘Termite’: Sirshendu Mukhopadhyay’s first novel tapped into urban alienation and existential drift
item.description: A new translation of the Bengali novel presents the protagonist’s acute indifference and his apparent lack of humane feelings.
item.content:encoded:
There are some novels that quietly unsettle you long after you’ve put them down. Ghunpoka, Bengali writer Sirshendu Mukhopadhyay’s first novel from the 1960s – now available in a new English translation as Termite – is certainly one of them. A haunting exploration of urban alienation and the modern existential drift, on its first publication the novel announced the arrival of a writer who would go on to reshape the Bengali literary landscape, turning away from conventional social realism towards a deep, inward, often unsettling focus on the uneasy terrain of the modern mind.

Calcutta, a psychological condition

Tapas Kumar Sen’s translation brings this early work to a contemporary readership with great care. In doing so, it also reintroduces a particular moment in Bengali literary history – when the city, especially Calcutta, began to be experienced not merely as a setting but as a psychological condition.

At the centre of the novel is Shyam, a young man who has drifted from the village of Banikhara in Bikrampur into the restless, indifferent sprawl of Calcutta. Despite a deep respect for his parents, Shyam represents a generation at odds with institutional authority. item.title: How the Gujarati books of RF Sethna fed India’s appetite for books about Japan in the early 1900s
item.description: They were one of the many building blocks that helped Indians develop a better understanding of Japan and the Japanese.
item.content:encoded:
In his 1936 autobiography, Jawaharlal Nehru, the future prime minister of India, reccalls being deeply affected in his teenage years by the Russo-Japanese war of 1904-’05. “Japanese victories stirred up my enthusiasm and I waited eagerly for the papers for fresh news daily,” recounts Nehru, who was 14 at the time. “I invested in a large number of books on Japan and tried to read some of them.”

It was the first time that the country of Japan had caught the attention of the Indian public. Japan had emerged from over two centuries of self-imposed isolation in the 1850s. Though trade between the two countries commenced soon thereafter, very few people in India knew anything about Japan, its society and its culture at the start of the twentieth century.

While Nehru could easily find books in English written by European and American authors, most Indians struggled to find books in their own languages. At a time when the printed word was the only source of information, the few books and articles on Japan that had been published in the nineteenth century seemed inadequate and out of date.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party political campaign, on September 25 called on Opposition parties to boycott polls if they do not trust the Election Commission to hold free and fair polls.

Dipke contended that this was a logical inconsistency: why are they participating in exercises they contend are rigged? It is merely for their “political survival”, he claimed.

By participating in elections, Opposition parties help “maintain the illusion that they are free and fair”. But a boycott would deny Indian elections the legitimacy they now have, Dipke argued.

Dipke’s approach found support on social media. Among those who called for polls to be boycotted was former minister in the Narendra Modi Cabinet, RK Singh, who had resigned from the Bharatiya Janata party last year.

But even after several years of alleging irregularities in the electoral process, no Opposition party has so far given a serious thought to the idea of boycotting elections.

Some on social media defended Dipke’s approach, suggesting that boycotting elections would not mean merely sitting at home and doing nothing more. A boycott could result in new political movements being built, protests and mass mobilisation against the alleged irregularities in elections, they argued.

Apple has removed the offline messaging application Bitchat from its India App Store after a demand from the Ministry of Information Technology, developer Jack Dorsey said on Saturday.

The removal came months after reports that youth demonstrators at Jantar Mantar, who were protesting against alleged irregularities in the conduct of competitive examinations, had been using such applications amid temporary internet restrictions that had been imposed at the protest site.

From Friday, protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over concerns about the functioning of the Election Commission and its handling of the special intensive revision of electoral rolls were held in Delhi and Mumbai.

Bitchat is an open-source, decentralised messaging application that allows nearby users to communicate without mobile data, Wi-Fi, phone numbers or centralised servers. It uses Bluetooth Low Energy to connect nearby phones, with each device capable of relaying messages to others and thereby extending the network’s reach. Private messages are end-to-end encrypted, and the application does not require users to create accounts or provide persistent identifiers.

While removal from the App Store does not delete Bitchat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates.

In July, the Union Home Ministry asked software platform GitHub to remove the repositories for Bitchat citing security concerns, according to a notice shared by Dorsey.

item.title: ‘Fusion cooking is an extension of imagination, memories, experiences’: Cookbook writer Rohini Rana
item.description: Rana is the author of ‘The Rana Cookbook’ and ‘Memories on a Platter’.
item.content:encoded:
Rohini Rana, affectionately known as Dolly, is a writer, culinary historian, and entrepreneur who is especially interested in preserving the rich culinary traditions of South Asia. She was born into the royal family of Awagarh in Uttar Pradesh and married into Nepal’s Rana family. Her travel, restaurant and social work, and her husband’s job in the army have deeply informed her writing.

Her books, The Rana Cookbook: Recipes from the Palaces of Nepal and The Nepal Cookbook: 108 Regional Recipes, documented royal and regional Nepali foodways with rare care and depth. Her latest book, Memories on a Platter: My Fusion Cookbook, brings together Indian, Nepali and global influences gathered through a life of movement, memory and hospitality, offering recipes that honour heritage while speaking to the modern palate.

Rana’s journey is a reminder that movement can also be a form of becoming. The book and author show us how food, memory and feminine resilience can exist gracefully on a platter. Her journey reminded me that a peripatetic life, one lived across postings, homes, cultures, kitchens and worlds, seasons a woman and makes her observant.

item.title: Ramachandra Guha: A century after Gandhi described the four pillars of swaraj, how do they hold up?
item.description: He pressed for equal rights for Dalits, women and minorities, an economic model that is equitable and sustainable, and the cultivation of non-violence.
item.content:encoded:
Mahatma Gandhi spent the last three decades of his life battling for his country’s freedom from British colonial rule. In this time, he rarely wrote or spoke about what he felt a free India should look like. However, in March 1922, he offered a short, succinct definition of swaraj that is worth revisiting today. Here is what he said:

“Removal of untouchability, manufacture of khaddar, Hindu-Muslim unity, cultivation of non-violence are not measures of a temporary nature. They are the four pillars on which the structure of swaraj must for ever rest. Take away any one of them and it must topple down.”

Let us unpack this statement and gloss each of its four elements.

We may take “removal of untouchability” to stand more broadly for the pursuit of social justice, which of course includes removing not just the inequalities of caste but also of gender. Unlike the other savarna leaders of the Congress – Nehru, Patel, Bose, et al – Gandhi was keenly aware of how the prevalence of untouchability undermined the Indian case for freedom. He therefore called it a “sin”, and those who practised it the “Dyers of Hinduism”.

item.title: Nigerian legend King Sunny Adé took African pop music to the world’s stage
item.description: The ‘King of Jùjú’ embodies an impressive blend of cultural grounding, musical innovation, entrepreneurial insight and global acclaim.
item.content:encoded:
Sunday Adeniyi Adegeye, known as King Sunny Adé, is 80 this year. He has devoted more than 60 years of his life to influencing Nigeria’s popular music and promoting the unique sounds of jùjú music.

Jùjú is a Nigerian musical tradition that combines intricate rhythms, percussion, guitars, talking drums, call-and-response and Yoruba oral culture. It’s not only entertainment but a vehicle for expressing cultural identity, transmitting proverbs and praise traditions, and social life commentary.

Sunny Adé’s career embodies an impressive blend of cultural grounding, musical innovation, entrepreneurial insight and global acclaim. From his beginnings in Lagos to his rise as the globally celebrated “King of Jùjú”, his story is intertwined with the development of contemporary African popular music.

As a social philosopher, I regard Sunny Adé’s music as a tool for social change. This is because it transforms cultural expression into a medium of moral reflection and social engagement. His music communicates values such as communal responsibility, respect, humility, peace, diligence and integrity. It also draws attention to the social problems confronting Nigerian society.

I’ve argued that Sunny Adé’s music addresses social challenges, preserves Yoruba identity and promotes civic awareness, national unity and moral renewal.

item.title: ‘Swan Song’: Princess Diana’s brother’s book is icy in its contempt for the British royal family
item.description: Charles Spencer casts King Charles, then the Prince of Wales, as a petulant child and ‘bellowing buffoon jealous of Diana’s star power’.
item.content:encoded:
Revenge is a dish best served cold, so the saying goes. Charles Spencer’s new memoir, Swan Song, arrives nearly three decades after his sister Diana’s death, and it is icy in its contempt for both the British tabloid media and the “arrogance and entitlement” of the royal family.

Dedicated to “all those who have lost a sibling”, and billed as revealing “the true framework of Diana’s life”, the memoir has been marketed as “the most intimate, loving and honest portrait” of Diana yet.

However, the book is as much about Spencer as it is about Diana. Over 350 pages, his litany of grievances swamps the loving tribute he ostensibly set out to write. King Charles, then the Prince of Wales, is cast as a petulant child and “bellowing buffoon” who was “always extremely jealous of Diana’s star power”.

Among the most damaging claims is that Charles was “giddily elated” on learning of Diana’s death, a reaction Spencer attributes to Charles’ “pent-up contempt for Diana and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death”, as well as what he sees as Charles’s relief at finally being free to marry the woman he loved.

“Rest assured,” Charles allegedly hissed, “we’ll forget [Diana] soon enough!”

item.title: Kolkata film institute suspends classes for sixth day after campus violence
item.description: Students are continuing their ‘academic boycott’, demanding the arrest of those responsible for injuring six of them on September 27.
item.content:encoded:
Classes at the Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute in Kolkata were suspended for the sixth day on Saturday as students continued their “academic boycott” over an alleged attack by members of a Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh-affiliated organisation on the campus, reported PTI.

The RSS, a Hindutva organisation, is the ideological parent of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

On September 27, at least six students were injured after being attacked for objecting to an event organised by members of the RSS-affiliated consumer group Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat.

The students’ union had stated that it was not informed about the event before the institute gave permission.

Poorvi Bondre, a member of the union, told Deutsche Welle that students confronted participants of the event after learning that the organisers were affiliated with the RSS and using the event to “promote its agenda” on campus.

“They called us anti-nationals and Naxals and attacked us with knives,” Bondre said.

Some students were also chased while others had their clothes torn and phones forcibly taken, the union had stated

Students have since been boycotting classes, demanding heightened security on campus and that those responsible for the violence be arrested, reported PTI.

The Kolkata Police is reportedly deployed outside the main gate of the campus.

The protest in Mumbai was called by the political campaign. Dipke had sought permission to demonstrate at Shivaji Park, but the police had denied it on September 27. Following this, he had said that the Cockroach Janta Party would launch a “jail bharo andolan”, or mass voluntary arrest movement.

No one was detained during the protest in Mumbai on Friday. The demonstration coincided with protests held at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, where the police detained more than 700 persons.

The protesters have raised concerns about the functioning of the Election Commission and its handling of the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

item.title: Prashant Bhushan, AISA’s Neha Bora detained at Jantar Mantar on day 2 of protest against CEC
item.description: Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal had also marched to the site of the demonstration, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
item.content:encoded:
Lawyer Prashant Bhushan, activist Yogendra Yadav and All India Students’ Association chief Neha Bora were among those detained at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on Saturday during a protest to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

This is the second consecutive day that demonstrations were held at Jantar Mantar demanding action against Kumar.

The protesters have raised concerns about the functioning of the Election Commission and its handling of the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

On Friday, Bora, Aam Aadmi Party’s Atishi and Saurabh Bharadwaj, and Rashtriya Janata Dal MP Manoj Kumar Jha were among the nearly 700 protesters whom the Delhi Police had detained from Jantar Mantar. All persons detained were reportedly released later in the day.

On Saturday, along with Bora, Yadav and Bhushan, Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal marched to Jantar Mantar.

The police have said that permission has not been granted for any demonstration and that orders prohibiting a gathering of five or more persons under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita remain in force in the New Delhi district.

The authorities had on Friday also suspended internet services in areas around Jantar Mantar, while the main protest area was barricaded.

item.title: ‘Love, fear, and a pursuit of fun’: What made Diksha Basu write a motherhood memoir
item.description: ‘This book began as my love letter to my daughters, and then it became a love letter to my mother.’
item.content:encoded:
I am a fiction writer. I find fiction safe, escapist, protective – a barrier against the world. It’s true, of course, that all fiction comes from reality and mine is no exception but I can always use an excuse with fiction when needed. When The Windfall was published, my mother insisted she saw my father on the pages and my father insisted he saw my mother on the pages. I quickly insisted neither of them was on the pages.

And now I sit on the eve of publishing my first longform nonfiction on one of the most vulnerable topics in the world – motherhood. And I have nowhere to hide. I find myself wondering why I wrote this book.

The now

Perhaps I wrote it out of self-defence. My daughters (currently eight and nine) and I do not yet have an emotionally complex relationship. There are emotions, there are fights, and there is growth and mirroring and a foreshadowing of the complications to come, but adolescence, while lurking, has not quite arrived yet. item.title: Uttarakhand: ‘Mohammed’ Deepak gets bail day after he was arrested for allegedly assaulting trader
item.description: The Dehradun gym owner was directed to furnish three bonds of Rs 50,000 each, assuring that he would not cause any breach of peace over the next six months.
item.content:encoded:
An Uttarakhand court on Friday granted bail to Dehradun gym owner Deepak Kumar, a day after he was arrested for allegedly assaulting a trader, reported PTI.

Kumar had in January opposed the harassment of an elderly Muslim shopkeeper by alleged Bajrang Dal members. When the group questioned him, he had told them his name was “Mohammad Deepak”. He later explained that he intended to convey that he was an Indian and that everyone is equal before the law.

On Thursday, Sanjeev Tonk, a businessman, alleged that Kumar had abused and assaulted him for a comment he had made on one of the social media posts by the gym owner.

Kumar had purportedly uploaded a social media post about the Ujjain municipal authority demolishing a portion of a mosque as part of a road-widening project ahead of the Hindu religious gathering called the Simhastha Kumbh Mela.

The court on Friday granted bail to Kumar after asking him to furnish three bonds of Rs 50,000 each, assuring that he would not cause any breach of peace over the next six months, reported The Indian Express.

item.title: India proposal to end Russia war ‘most comprehensive’, says Ukraine
item.description: New Delhi had ‘for the first time’ signalled its willingness to ‘play a role’, said Kyiv.
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Friday said that India’s proposal to end the war with Russia is the “most comprehensive” and broad, reported RBC-Ukraine.

“For the first time, India has signalled its willingness to play a role,” he told reporters.

Sybiha said that Kyiv had also received proposals from Egypt, Turkey and the United States.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 triggered the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.

The Ukrainian foreign minister said that his country was prepared to agree to an energy and agricultural truce in the Black Sea. However, any energy truce must entail a cessation of attacks on all power infrastructure, including facilities at ports, he was quoted as saying.

Several vessels, including many with Indians on board, have been struck in the Black Sea in recent months.

Sybiha also said that Kyiv was considering an unconditional ceasefire along the frontline with Russia, RBC-Ukraine reported.

On Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi had “very good ideas” for finding mutually acceptable solutions to end the conflict.

However, Putin ruled out an end to long-range strikes as Moscow intensified aerial attacks on Kyiv.

“We are told: ‘Let them stop striking your refineries, and you will stop striking their ships,’” Putin said. “It is simply ridiculous.”
